check: Write down exactly what is changing: domain, protocol, URL structure, CMS, design, hosting
why: Each kind of change carries different risks and needs different steps. A hosting move with no URL changes needs no redirects; a domain change needs redirects and the Change of Address tool.
how: List every change in the Notes column. If URLs don't change, follow Google's 'moving hosting without URL changes' guide instead of this full process.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Change one thing at a time where you can
why: Google recommends moving domain first and redesigning later, for example. Stacking changes makes it hard to tell what caused a drop.
how: Agree the order of changes with stakeholders. If everything must ship together, plan extra benchmarking and monitoring.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Decide whether to move everything at once or in sections
why: Google recommends moving small and medium sites all at once, and suggests large sites can move section by section to spot problems early.
how: Size the site from a crawl and the sitemap. For large sites, pick a test section that changes rarely and isn't driven by unpredictable events.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Pick a launch window in a quieter traffic period, with a freeze and a rollback plan
why: Fewer users meet any problems, and more server capacity is left for Googlebot's extra crawling after the move.
how: Check seasonality in analytics. Avoid launches before weekends or holidays. Agree a content and code freeze, who can sign off, and how to roll back.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Set expectations: rankings fluctuate, and a medium site can take a few weeks or more to settle
why: Google says visibility may fluctuate while it recrawls; medium sites can take a few weeks or more for new URLs to replace old ones, larger sites longer. Agreeing this upfront avoids panic decisions.
how: Share the timeline and the KPIs you'll report on (indexed URLs, organic clicks by section, key conversions) with stakeholders before launch.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Keep the old domain registered (at least a year, ideally for good) with a valid TLS certificate
why: Google recommends paying for the old domain for at least a year so nobody else can buy and misuse it. Redirects from https:// URLs also need a working certificate on the old host.
how: Check the registrar renewal date and auto-renew. Confirm the old host keeps serving HTTPS long enough to return the redirects.
source_label: Google Help: Change of Address tool

check: Crawl the old site in full and save the export
why: The crawl is your record of what existed: URLs, status codes, titles, H1s, H2s, meta descriptions, canonicals, hreflang and structured data. It also feeds the fuzzy-matching notebook.
how: Screaming Frog (or similar) with the Internal: HTML export; keep Address, Title 1, H1-1, H2-1, H2-2 and Meta Description 1 for redirect matching. Store the file with the launch date.

check: Export Search Console and analytics data per URL
why: You need before-and-after numbers by page and section, and the old property's data becomes harder to compare once URLs change.
how: Search Console: page and query performance for the last 16 months, Page indexing report, Links report. GA4: landing pages with sessions and key events.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: List every old URL that needs a decision, including images, PDFs and video
why: Google suggests starting with your most important URLs and including embedded content such as images, videos, PDFs, JavaScript and CSS, which may be getting traffic or links.
how: Combine sitemaps, the crawl, server logs, analytics landing pages, the Search Console Links report and a CMS export. Deduplicate into the Redirect map tab.
learn_label: 404 and redirect mapping with fuzzy matching
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Export the pages with backlinks and save the list of linking sites
why: Old URLs with links pass their value on through permanent redirects. You'll also contact the most valuable linking sites after launch.
how: Search Console > Links (top linked pages and linking sites), plus Ahrefs or Semrush if you have them. Add referring domains to the Redirect map.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Record your AI search and SERP feature baseline
why: Migrations can break the URLs AI assistants and SERP features cite. A baseline shows whether you lost citations, rich results or a knowledge panel link.
how: Note rich results by type (Search Console Enhancements), AI Overview appearances for key queries, and a quick citation check in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini for your top questions.
learn_label: Your rank tracker is lying to you about AI search

check: Map every old URL to its closest equivalent new URL, one to one where possible
why: Relevant one-to-one redirects keep users and signals on the right page. Google recommends a full old-to-new mapping for any move beyond a simple domain swap.
how: Use the Redirect map tab. For a straight domain change with identical paths, a wildcard rule may be enough; still test a sample.
learn_label: 404 and redirect mapping with fuzzy matching
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Draft the map at scale with fuzzy matching, then review it
why: Matching hundreds or thousands of URLs by hand takes days. Fuzzy matching on URL, title, H1, H2 and meta description shortlists the best candidates in minutes.
how: Under about 300 URLs: the MLforSEO fuzzy matching Google Sheets template. Larger: the triple fuzzy matching notebook (old vs new crawl) or the 404 mapping notebook. Paste results into the Redirect map tab.
source_label: Fuzzy matching Google Sheets template

check: Review every partial or low-scoring match by hand
why: String similarity has no understanding of meaning or intent. Two similar slugs can be different products; a strong score can still be wrong for the user.
how: Sort the Redirect map by Similarity. Validate a sample to choose your own threshold, accept only above it, and set a Decision for everything below. Matches where several algorithms agree are safer.
learn_label: 404 and redirect mapping with fuzzy matching

check: Don't redirect lots of old URLs to the home page or an unrelated page
why: Google may treat irrelevant redirects as soft 404s, and they confuse users. Redirecting several old pages to one new page that consolidates their content is fine.
how: Check the Flags column in the Redirect map for 'Home page redirect'. For content with no equivalent, choose 410 or 404 instead.
learn_label: 404 and redirect mapping with fuzzy matching
source_label: Google: HTTP status codes and soft 404s

check: Content you're retiring returns 404 or 410
why: Google's guide asks for a 404 or 410 on deleted content rather than a redirect to something unrelated.
how: Set Decision to '410 Gone' or '404' in the Redirect map. Make sure the 404 page returns a real 404 status code.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Plan server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) straight to the final URL
why: Permanent redirects don't lose PageRank. Googlebot follows up to 10 hops, but Google advises redirecting to the final destination directly, and ideally no more than 3 hops.
how: Agree the implementation with developers: server config (.htaccess, nginx), CDN rules or the CMS. Client-side (JavaScript or meta refresh) redirects are a last resort.
source_label: Google: redirects and Google Search

check: Update existing redirects so they point at the new final URLs
why: Redirects from earlier migrations will otherwise chain through the old site (old > older > new).
how: Export current redirect rules, run them through the same mapping, and rewrite each to point directly at the new destination.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Keep staging out of search, and list exactly what to unblock at launch
why: Staging sites get indexed by accident. Google's guide notes that if you block crawling or use noindex during development, you need a ready list of what to remove at launch.
how: Password-protect staging (HTTP authentication) where possible. If you use noindex or robots.txt blocks, record each one in Notes so none are left behind.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Crawl staging and compare it with the old-site crawl
why: Missing pages, empty titles, lost H1s, dropped structured data or thinner content show up in a side-by-side comparison before they cost traffic.
how: Crawl staging (with authentication) and compare URL counts, titles, H1s, meta descriptions, word counts and structured data by template with the benchmark crawl.

check: Every new URL has a self-referencing canonical, and hreflang uses the new URLs
why: Canonicals or hreflang still pointing at old or staging URLs send mixed signals about which version to index.
how: Crawl staging and check canonical and hreflang targets. None should point to the staging host or the old domain.
source_label: Google: canonical URLs

check: Internal links point straight at new URLs, not through redirects
why: Updating internal links reduces redirect load and helps Google find the new URLs faster.
how: Use the mapping to find-and-replace links in content, navigation, footers and templates. Crawl staging and filter internal links returning 3xx.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: A sitemap of the new URLs is ready, plus one of the old URLs
why: Submitting the new sitemap helps Google discover the new URLs. Google's guide also suggests submitting the old-URL sitemap so you can watch old URLs drop out (redirect warnings there are expected).
how: Generate the new XML sitemap (indexable 200 URLs only). Keep the old sitemap file from the benchmark.
source_label: Google: build a sitemap

check: The new robots.txt is ready and keeps your AI crawler decisions
why: A robots.txt copied from staging can block the whole site. Rebuilds also tend to drop rules for AI search crawlers (OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Claude-SearchBot), or a CDN default may start blocking them.
how: Prepare the production robots.txt in advance and diff it against the old one. Check CDN bot settings on the new setup. If you publish llms.txt, update its URLs.
learn_label: Your robots.txt might be the silent killer of your AI traffic
source_label: Google: robots.txt introduction

check: Structured data uses new URLs, and entity @id values stay stable
why: Markup often hard-codes URLs (url, logo, sameAs, breadcrumbs, @id). If @id values change, the connections between your entities break.
how: Search templates and the CMS for the old domain in JSON-LD. Keep @id values unchanged, or map them deliberately if they were built from page URLs.

check: Analytics, tag manager and Search Console verification work on the new templates
why: Missing tracking on launch day leaves a hole in your data. Search Console verification can break if the HTML file or meta tag isn't carried over.
how: Test tags on staging. Verify both old and new sites in Search Console, including all variants (www and non-www, http and https).
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: The server and CDN can handle extra crawling
why: Google says it will temporarily crawl the new site more heavily than usual after a move. Slow or failing responses slow down the whole migration.
how: Warn your host for large sites. Make sure rate limits and WAF rules allow verified Googlebot and Bingbot.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: If the new domain was bought second-hand, check its history
why: A previous owner may have left manual actions or URL removal requests in place.
how: Verify the new domain in Search Console and check Manual actions and Removals before launch.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Test the full redirect map on staging
why: Mistakes in rules (wrong destinations, loops, chains, missing trailing slashes, lost query strings) are cheapest to fix before launch.
how: Crawl the list of old URLs against staging in list mode with redirects followed. Fill in Status code, Hops and Final URL returns 200 in the Redirect map.
learn_label: 404 and redirect mapping with fuzzy matching

check: Switch on the redirects and remove the staging blocks
why: Leftover noindex tags or robots.txt blocks are one of the most common reasons a new site fails to get indexed.
how: Deploy redirects; remove noindex and authentication; publish the production robots.txt. Spot-check with URL Inspection.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Crawl every old URL: each returns 301 or 308 in one hop to a URL that returns 200
why: Google frequently sees redirects pointing to wrong or non-existent URLs. A list crawl catches them in minutes.
how: List-mode crawl of all old URLs with redirects followed. Filter for chains, loops, 4xx and 5xx destinations and anything not matching the Final destination column.
learn_label: 404 and redirect mapping with fuzzy matching
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Domain or subdomain change: submit Change of Address for every verified variant
why: The tool tells Google to prefer the new site and forwards signals for 180 days. You don't need it for HTTP to HTTPS, www to non-www, or path changes on the same domain.
how: Search Console > Settings > Change of Address on the old domain-level property. Repeat for www, non-www and any subdomains, even unused ones.
source_label: Google Help: Change of Address tool

check: Submit sitemaps in Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, and ping IndexNow
why: Sitemaps speed up discovery in Google. Bing Webmaster Tools has its own site move tool, and IndexNow notifies Bing and other participating engines of changed URLs.
how: Submit the new sitemap (and the old-URL sitemap) in both tools. Use Bing's site move tool for domain changes. Send old and new URLs through IndexNow.
source_label: Bing Webmaster Tools

check: Re-upload any disavow file to the new property
why: Google recommends re-uploading the old site's disavow file to the new Search Console property if you used one.
how: Download it from the old property's disavow tool and upload to the new one.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Inspect one URL from each key template
why: Confirms Googlebot sees the right rendered content, canonical and indexability on the live site.
how: Search Console > URL Inspection > Test live URL for the home page, a category, a product or service page and an article.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Monitor indexing, crawl stats and errors every day for the first two weeks
why: Old URLs should drop out while new ones are indexed. Spikes in 404s, 5xx errors or 'Page with redirect' on new URLs need fixing fast.
how: Search Console: Page indexing (old and new properties), Sitemaps, Crawl stats. Server logs: Googlebot status codes on old and new URLs.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Fix 404s on old URLs that have traffic or links within days
why: Each one is lost value and a broken journey. The 404 notebook can map a new batch of broken URLs to live pages quickly.
how: Pull 404s from Search Console, logs and the analytics 404 page. Map them with the Redirect map tab or the 404 mapping notebook and deploy in batches.

check: Update the links you control and ask for the important external ones to change
why: Redirects are slow for users. Google suggests updating profile links, ad campaigns and high-value backlinks to point straight at new URLs.
how: Update social profiles, Business Profile, Wikidata 'official website', Crunchbase, email templates, ads and partner pages. Contact the top linking sites from your benchmark list.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Compare organic traffic and conversions with the benchmark by section
why: Sitewide totals hide problems. Section or template comparisons show exactly where something broke.
how: Weekly: clicks, impressions and key events by section, against the same weeks last year and the pre-launch baseline. Annotate the launch date in GA4 and your reports.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Recheck AI answers and SERP features for your key queries
why: Assistants and knowledge panels can keep citing old URLs for a while. Checking shows whether they now point to working, correct pages.
how: Rerun the baseline questions from M11. Check rich results in Search Console Enhancements and that your knowledge panel shows the new website.
learn_label: Your rank tracker is lying to you about AI search

check: Keep redirects for at least a year, ideally permanently
why: Google recommends keeping redirects as long as possible, generally at least one year, so it can recrawl and transfer signals, and suggests users benefit from keeping them indefinitely.
how: Document redirects somewhere other than one developer's memory (this workbook). Add a calendar reminder before any server or CMS change that could drop them.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Remove the old-URL sitemap once old URLs have dropped out
why: Once Google uses the new sitemap, the old one has done its job.
how: When the old sitemap shows close to zero indexed URLs in Search Console, remove it.
source_label: Google: how to move a site (URL changes)

check: Review results at 3, 6 and 12 months and write down what you learned
why: A short write-up makes the next migration faster and shows stakeholders the outcome.
how: Compare traffic, indexed URLs and conversions by section with the benchmark. Note what went wrong, what you'd repeat and any redirects still pending.
